Q.  PS6.4 Describe the treatment of depression including behavioral and pharmacologic therapy.

Treatment of depression
Both drug and psychotherapy (e.g., cognitive behavioral therapy, interpersonal therapy) are effective in the treatment of depression either
alone or in combination. Medication alone also can relieve symptoms. However, the combined approach generally provides the patient with
the quickest and most sustained response.
Drug treatment (pharmacotherapy)
All antidepressants are potentially effective in patients whose depression is secondary to medical illness, as well as those in whom it is the
primary problem. They are effective in moderate and severe depression. Usually, 2–6 weeks at a therapeutic dose level are needed to observe
a clinical response. Commonly used antidepressants are listed in Table 20.5.
Psychological treatments
• Mild-to-moderate depression: Both cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and interpersonal therapy (IPT) are as effective.
• Severe depression: Antidepressant drugs are preferred.
Nonpharmacologic treatments
• Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT): Highly effective for depression and may have a more rapid onset of action than drug treatments. ECT

may be indicated if patient is suicidal or worried about side effects from medications.
• Other magnetic and electrical stimulatory methods like r-TMS

Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD)
z It is a chronic state associated with uncontrollable excessive and free floating anxiety and worry persisting for minimum

6 months.
z Symptoms: It is associated with somatic symptoms of muscle tension and bowel disturbance, sleep disturbance, and

difficulty concentrating or mind going blank.

Panic (Paroxysmal) Disorder
z Panic disorder is defined as the occurrence of recurrent unexpected attacks of intense anxiety that include marked

physical symptoms, such as tachycardia, chest pain, hyperventilation, dizziness, trembling, numbness, and sweating.
z Panic disorder may occur with or without agoraphobia (avoidance of situations where a person may feel trapped and

unable to escape). A discrete period of intense fear or discomfort which develops abruptly and reaches a peak within
10 minutes. In between the attacks, patient is free from anxiety.

z Age of onset for panic disorder varies but lies between late adolescence and mid-30s.
z Patients have persistent concern of having attack and they worry about the implications of attack.

Phobic Anxiety Disorder
A phobia is an abnormal or excessive, persistent and disproportionate fear of an object or situation that presents little or no
actual danger to the person. It causes avoidance of it (e.g., excessive fear of dying in an air crash leading to avoidance of flying).
Phobic responses can develop to general medical procedures, such as venipuncture.

Types of Phobia
z Specific phobia: Fear of specific situation/object.

Post-traumatic Stress Disorder
z It is characterized by the re-experiencing (recurrent bouts) of an extremely traumatic event accompanied by the symptoms

of increased arousal and by avoidance of stimuli associated with trauma.
z The traumatic event (e.g., a military experience, a physical or sexual assault, a motor vehicle accident, a natural disaster)

involved may have caused death or near death experience or serious injury to self or others.
z Typically, patients re-experience the traumatic event (e.g., nightmares, flashbacks intrusive recollections), engage in

avoidance of trauma or talk of trauma, or recollections of stimuli associated with the sentinel trauma. Patients experience
increased autonomic reactivity, such as hypervigilance, irritability, insomnia startle responses, etc.

Classification of PTSD
z Acute PTSD: Symptoms begin within 3 months of trauma or the duration of symptoms is <3 months.
z Chronic (or delayed) PTSD: Symptoms start >3 months after trauma (delayed) or persist for 3 months or longer.
z With delayed onset: 6 months have passed between the traumatic event and the onset of symptoms.
Management: Psychological (Eye movement desensitization psychotherapy) and pharmacological (antidepressants and

Investigations and Diagnosis
Diagnosis may be apparent from the history or may be made when the patient presents with a complication.

Laboratory Toxicology

Treatment of Substance-related Disorders
Biological treatment: Pharmacologic intervention to ameliorate psychological or physical symptoms.
z Agonist substitution: Safe drug with a similar chemical composition as the abused drug (e.g., methadone for heroin

addiction).
z Antagonistic treatment: Drugs that block Treatment of Substance-related Disorders ck or counteract the positive effects

of substances (e.g., naltrexone for opiate and alcohol problems).
z Aversive treatment: Drugs that make the injection of abused substances extremely unpleasant (e.g., disulfiram for

alcoholism and silver nitrate for nicotine addiction).
Psychosocial treatment
z Community support programs: These are strongly encouraged.
z Emotional reassurance and providing a structured and secure environment.
z Components of comprehensive treatment and prevention programs: Individual and group therapy, aversion therapy and

convert sensitization, contingency management, community reinforcement, relapse prevention, and preventative efforts
via education.

Main Categories of Substances
z Depressants: Result in behavioral sedation (e.g., alcohol, sedatives, anxiolytic, and hypnotic drugs).
z Stimulants: Increase alertness and elevate mood (e.g., cocaine, nicotine, caffeine, and amphetamines).
z Opiates: Primarily produce analgesia and euphoria (e.g., heroin, morphine, codeine, and brown sugar).
z Hallucinogens: Alter sensory perception [e.g., marijuana (cannabis), lysergic acid diethylamide, phencyclidine]
z Club/rave party drugs: Cause anterograde amnesia (e.g., gamma hexane butyrate, flunitrazepam, and ketamine)

Q.  PS4.1, 4.2 and 4.4 Describe etiology, clinical features and management of alcohol use disorders.

ALCOHOL
Consumption of alcohol when associated with social, psychological, and physical problems constitutes alcohol use disorder.

Etiology
Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant. It influences several neurotransmitter systems, mainly GABA (inhibition of
behavior) but also glutamate system and serotonin system.

Alcohol Dependence
It is characterized by a problematic pattern of alcohol use leading to clinically significant impairment or distress, as manifested
by multiple psychosocial, behavioral, or physiologic features.
Features of alcohol dependence
z Loss of control: Engaging in risky behaviors while under the influence.
z Compulsive preoccupation: Worrying compulsively about getting a “fix” and spending a lot of their time thinking about

the drug.
z Continued use of alcohol despite negative consequences: Losing control of the ability to monitor how much and how

often the user takes their drug.
z Loss of motivation: Losing interest in activities that the user enjoyed prior to addiction.
z Desire to stop drinking, but inability to do so.
z Excessive time spent getting or using alcohol, or recovering from its effects.
z Craving, or preoccupation with drinking.
z Problems stemming from alcohol use; ignoring those problems; drinking despite obvious hazards, including physical

danger.
z Retreating from important work, family, or social activities and roles.
z Tolerance: The need to drink more and more alcohol to feel the same effects, or the ability to drink more than other people

without getting drunk.
z Withdrawal symptoms: After stopping or cutting back on drinking, symptoms are anxiety, sweating, trembling, trouble

sleeping, nausea or vomiting, and, in severe cases, physical seizures and hallucinations. The person may drink to relieve
or avoid such symptoms.

Consequences of alcohol harmful use/dependence
Neuropsychiatric
• Depression, suicide
• Alcohol relieves anxiety in the short term, dependence can develop in long-term use
• Alcoholic hallucinosis: auditory hallucinations
• Alcoholic “blackouts”: Amnesia for events that occurred during bouts of intoxication in very heavy alcoholic drinkers.
• Alcohol withdrawal (discussed below): Maximum symptoms usually develop 2–3 days after the last drink and can produce seizures

(“rum fits”).
• Delirium tremens: It is a form of delirium found with severe alcohol withdrawal.
• Neurological: Peripheral neuropathy, dementia, cerebral hemorrhage, cerebellar degeneration, Marchiafava-Bignami syndrome, subacute

combined degeneration of the cord myopathy, ventricular enlargement, and cognitive impairment.
• Wernicke’s encephalopathy: Global confusion, nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia
• Korsakoff’s syndrome: Short-term memory deficits, confabulation
• Alcoholic dementia: It is a global cognitive impairment which may resemble Alzheimer’s disease. It does not progress and may improve

if the patient abstains from alcohol.
• Indirect effects on brain: It may be due to head injury subdural hematoma, hypoglycemia, and encephalopathy.
Medical
• Hepatic: Fatty change and cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma
• Gastrointestinal: Esophagitis, esophageal varices, Mallory-Weiss syndrome, esophageal carcinoma, gastritis, malabsorption, pancreatitis,

and parotid enlargement
• Skin: Palmar erythema, spider naevi, Dupuytren’s contractures, and telangiectasias
• Cardiac: Cardiomyopathy and hypertension

Disturbed sleep is one of the most frequent health complaints.

Sleep disorders can be of various types:

Insomnia
Insomnia is the complaint of inability to sleep long enough or maintain sleep despite the patient having adequate amount
of time to devote to sleep. It is associated with impairment of daytime functioning or mood symptoms.

Insomnia can be classified according to the nature of sleep disruption and the duration of the complaint. Most insomnia
patients present with two or more of these symptoms:
z Sleep onset insomnia: Difficulty falling asleep.
z Sleep maintenance insomnia: Frequent or sustained awakenings.
z Sleep offset insomnia: Early morning awakenings or frequent nocturnal awakenings.

Common causes of insomnia
Primary sleep disorders:
• Idiopathic insomnia • Periodic leg movements • Restless legs syndrome
Secondary sleep disorders:
• Psychiatric or psychological problems: Mood disorders (e.g., mania, depressive, and anxiety disorders); delirium and dementia
• Use or misuse of drug/substance abuse: Consumption or discontinuation of drugs/substances. Withdrawal of addictive drug (e.g.,

alcohol and benzodiazepines); stimulant drugs (e.g., caffeine, nicotine, and amphetamines); prescribed drugs (corticosteroids and
dopamine agonists)

• Physical/medical disorders: Chronic pain (e.g., carpal tunnel syndrome); nocturia (e.g., prostatism); malnutrition, chronic obstructive
pulmonary disease, asthma, menopause, and neurologic disorders.

Consequences
z Depression may cause insomnia, and insomnia may cause depression.
z Can heighten the perception of pain.
z May be associated with:

 Development of endocrine disturbances.
 Increased risk for hypertension or cardiovascular disease.
 Increased risk for motor vehicle accidents and occupational errors.

Treatment
z Behavioral therapy is effective but may be time-consuming. These include: Relaxation techniques and cognitive behavior

therapy.
z Other measures include: Decreasing alcohol intake, to have early supper, daily exercise, and hot bath prior to going to bed

and routine going to bed at the same time.
z Pharmacologic treatment:

 Benzodiazepines (e.g., temazepam, triazolam, estazolam, and eszopiclone) for sleep-maintenance insomnia.

NARCOLEPSY
Etiology
z Loss of orexin (hypocretin) signaling
z Strong genetic/HLA association: HLADQB1*0602 haplotype is present in 95% of patients with cataplexy and in 96% of

those with orexin deficiency.

Clinical Features
The classic “narcolepsy tetrad” consists of four main clinical features:
1. Excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) occurring almost daily for at least 3 months that interferes with functioning plus

three specific symptoms related to an intrusion of REM sleep characteristics. Sleep attack is the most common symptom.
2. Cataplexy (pathognomonic sign): Sudden weakness or loss of muscle tone without loss of consciousness, usually

precipitated by loud noise, laughter, or other intense emotions.
3. Hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations: Hypnagogic hallucinations (hallucinations occur as the patient is going to

sleep) or hypnopompic hallucinations (hallucinations upon awakening).
4. Sleep paralysis: Muscle paralysis upon awakening. It consists of episodes up to several minutes in duration of inability

to move and occasionally feeling unable to breathe despite being awake. Fragmented sleep is classically seen in
patients.

Diagnosis
z Electrographic evidence/multiple sleep latency test: Demonstration of rapid transition from wakefulness to sleep and

shortened REM sleep onset is confirmatory for the diagnosis. A mean sleep latency of ≤8 minutes and two or more sleep
onset REM periods (SOREMPs) on a

sleep) or hypnopompic hallucinations (hallucinations upon awakening).
4. Sleep paralysis: Muscle paralysis upon awakening. It consists of episodes up to several minutes in duration of inability

to move and occasionally feeling unable to breathe despite being awake. Fragmented sleep is classically seen in
patients.

Diagnosis
z Electrographic evidence/multiple sleep latency test: Demonstration of rapid transition from wakefulness to sleep and

shortened REM sleep onset is confirmatory for the diagnosis. A mean sleep latency of ≤8 minutes and two or more sleep
onset REM periods (SOREMPs) on a multiple sleep latency test (MSLT) is performed using standard techniques.

z HLA testing may also be useful.
z Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) hypocretin-1 concentration is low.

Treatment
Mainly symptomatic: Forced naps at a regular time of day is usually the treatment of choice.
Psychostimulants:
• Wake-promoting therapeutics: Modafinil is the drug of choice, principally because it has few side effects and has low addiction

potential. Older drugs such as methylphenidate or methamphetamine or dextroamphetamine are used as alternatives, particularly in
refractory patients.

• Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) help to suppress the REM sleep (e.g., protriptyline, imipramine, and clomipramine) or the selective
serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) [e.g., fluoxetine (10–20 mg/d)] or selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (e.g., venlafaxine)
can improve cataplexy.

• Gamma hydroxybutyrate (GHB) is effective in reducing daytime cataplectic episodes.
• Sodium oxybate, a sodium salt of GHB alone or combined with modafinil, can reduce sleep disruption significantly. It is administered

at night to help consolidate REM sleep and increase slow-wave sleep. It significantly reduces daytime sleepiness and also improves
cataplexy.

• Pitolisant, a histamine H3 receptor inverse agonist, is effective treatment for cataplexy and daytime sleepiness.
• Others: Selegiline, clomipramine, fluoxetine, and venlafaxine.

Circadian Rhythm Sleep Disorders
z Circadian rhythm sleep disorders (CRSDs) are mainly due to alterations of the circadian time-keeping system or

asynchrony between the endogenous circadian rhythm and external factors that affect the timing or duration of sleep.
z Wake-sleep schedule disorders fall into two categories:

1. Primary malfunction of the biologic clock per se
2. Secondary malfunction due to environmental effects on the underlying clock.

Example: Shift work type: Night shift or shift changes

Sleep-related Movement Disorders
These include restless leg syndrome and periodic limb movement disorder.

Restless Leg Syndrome (Willis-Ekbom Disease)
It is characterized by urge to move legs and patient usually complains of a variety of uncomfortable sensations in the legs
(e.g., pins and needles, creeping or crawling sensations, aching, itching, stabbing, heaviness, tension, burning, or coldness).
z Symptoms are usually experienced during periods of prolonged rest or inactivity.
z Symptoms are typically relieved only by movement or stimulation of the legs.
z The discomfort appears more prominent during evening and between midnight and 4 am.
z May disrupt sleep initiation.

Types
z Primary or idiopathic: Inherited as an autosomal dominant disorder.
z Secondary: To other causes, including iron deficiency, pregnancy, varicose vein or venous reflux, uremia, or folate

deficiency, peripheral neuropathy, radiculopathy rheumatoid arthritis, etc. It often develops suddenly and may be daily
from the very beginning.

Treatment
• Treatment of the underlying condition.
• First-line drugs: Dopamine agonists (e.g., pramipexole, carbidopa/levodopa or pergolide, and ropinirole) are the treatments of choice.
• Other drugs include quinine levodopa preparations, gabapentin, opiate agonists (e.g., oxycodone, codeine, propoxyphene oxycodone,

or methadone), benzodiazepines (e.g., clonazepam which often assists in staying asleep and reducing awakenings from the movements)
may also be effective. Anticonvulsants, such as gabapentin, often helpful in patients with painful sensations.

Periodic Limb Movement Disorder
z It is a repetitive, stereotyped limb movement and consists of 0.5- to 5.0-s extensions of the great toe and dorsiflexion of the foot.
z It occurs/recurs every 20–40 seconds during NREM sleep and each

episode lasts from minutes to hours. Treatment
z Movements often disrupt sleep and lead to daytime sleepiness. Dopaminergic medications or benzodiazepines.

ATTENTION DEFICIT HYPERACTIVITY DISORDER
z It is a disorder characterized by triad of hyperactivity, impulsivity, attention deficit manifesting at ≥2 contexts and having

its onset before 12 years of age. It is more common in boys.
z Etiology: Abnormality in information processing due to involvement of cortico-striatal-thalamo-cortical loop
z Clinical features include—inability to wait for their turn or to sit at one place, poor concentration, losing things easily,

poor scholastic performance despite normal IQ, etc.
z Management includes pharmacotherapy stimulants like methylphenidate and dextroamphetamine and nonstimulants

like atomoxetine, clonidine, and behavioral techniques like attention enhancing tasks, social skills training, and behavior
therapy.

Tic/Tourette Disorder
z Tourette syndrome (TS) is a neurological disorder characterized by repetitive, stereotyped, involuntary movements and

vocalizations called tics.
z It can be of four types:

1. Vocal tics: Throat clearing, grunting
2. Motor tics: Eye blinking, head nodding
3. Coprolalia: Blurting obscene words
4. Palilalia: Repeating words

z It can be managed by using antipsychotics like risperidone and haloperidol. Clonidine can also be used.
z Behavioral techniques include habit reversal and others.

AUTISTIC SPECTRUM DISORDER
z It was previously called pervasive developmental disorders to describe a group of disorders that shared similar

clinical features (i.e., abnormalities in reciprocal communication and repetitive stereotyped behaviors as core
features).

z Clinical features include self-absorbed child with poor eye to eye contact, lack of social smile, delayed milestones,
problems in attachment with parents and others, repetitive hand wringing, banging, etc.

z Management is mainly with psychotherapy (social skills training, speech and communication, behavioral) and
antipsychotics like risperidone and aripiprazole.

Childhood Depression

 Neutral stimulus (bell) + Unconditioned stimulus (food) = Unconditioned response (drool)
 After conditioning, neutral stimulus becomes conditioned stimulus to produce conditioned response (drool).

 Skinner’s operant conditioning (learning by re-inforcement/punishment) using rats and pigeons:
 Animal placed in operant chamber/skinner’s box was delivered food on doing a desired task, whereas shock was

delivered on doing undesired task. This was used to describe the effect of reinforcement and punishment on
behavioral change.

tidbits in 18 places while the chimp watched. Later, all four chimps were asked to search for hidden food.

 Experimental chimp ran directly to the nearby hidden places to find the food, without wandering around in
haphazardly like the other three chimps

 Theorists concluded that individuals develop cognitive maps of the environment and these cognitive maps form
the basis for one’s perceptions and expectations

Q.  Explain memory and its theories.
Memory is a process by which information is registered, retained in the brain, retrieved and recalled.

1378 CHAPTER 20: Psychiatry

Anatomical correlates of memory
z Prefrontal cortex stores of short term memories
z Frontal lobe stores semantic and episodic memories
z Motor cortex and cerebellum store procedural memories
z Temporal lobe: Processing of new short-term memory and formation and storage of long-term semantic and episodic memories
z Hippocampus: Formation of new long-term semantic and episodic memories
z Amygdala: Formation of new emotional memories

A. Theories of General Memory Function involves following processes:
 Encoding: Received sensory input is transformed into a code for storage
 Storage of encoded information into memory; short-term (lasts 20–30s without rehearsal) and long-term
 Retrieval: Gaining access to stored, coded information process

B. Atkinson, Shiffrin and Slavin’s information processing theory: Three components
1. Sensory register: Registering sensory information which can may be internal or external (via five sense organs)

 Unattended information is lost; paying attention shifts information from sensory register to working memory
2. Working memory: Processing the registered information based on past experiences, motivation, culture etc.

 Processing involves rehearsal/repetition to retain the information, associating with other information, organizing
for storage or discarding it.

 Information rehearsed/repeated more gets transferred to long-term memory
3. Long-term memory: Storing and retrieving the information. It can be further classified as:

 Explicit/Declarative memory: It requires to be consciously recalled. It can be further classified into episodic/
autobiographical memory (events in personal experience) and semantic memory (vocabulary, concepts, facts etc.)

 Implicit/Nondeclarative/Procedural memory: Does not require to be consciously recalled (e.g., memory for
procedures, skills and habits that are learnt).

C. Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch’s theory of tripartite working memory has four components:
1. Central Executive: Supervises and controls flow of information to and from the other three components (aka slave

systems). It also deals with cognitive tasks such as mental arithmetic and problem solving.
2. Visuo-spatial sketchpad (aka inner eye): Stores the information in visual or spatial form.
3. Phonological loop: Deals with written and spoken material; two types:

1. Acoustic/phonological stores: Deals with speech perception
2. Articulatory control process (acoustic loop): It is used to rehearse and store information from acoustic store.

4. Episodic Buffer: It links information across domains to form integrated units of verbal, spatial and visual information
with time sequencing (chronological ordering). It is linked to long term memory.

D. Craik and Lockhart’s depth of information processing theory of memory:
 Shallow processing of the appearance/physical form (structured) and sounds (phonemic)

 Leads to short term retention
 Deep processing of meaning of a word and relating it to similar word with similar meaning

 Involves elaborative rehearsal of information and hence leads better recall

Q.  Explain motivation and its theories.
Motivation refers to the driving forces guiding the persistent behavior directed towards particular goal:
z Drive/Push theory: Internal driving force pushes the individual to engage in behavior leading towards the goal aka

goal-directed behavior, which in turn reduces the intensity of driving force
z Incentive theory: Goals/Incentives acts as external pulling forces
z Opponent process theory: Individual is motivated to seek goals that give emotionally good feeling and avoid those that

give displeasure
z Optimum level theories: Individual is motivated to behave in such a way as to maintain an optimal level of arousal
z Maslow’s theory of self-actualization: Behavior motivated by the drive for satisfaction of a set of needs arranged in a

universal hierarchy to attain self-actualization (development of one’s full potential as a unique human being)
 Hierarchy of satisfaction of needs: physiological (hunger, thirst etc.), safety, love and belongingness, esteem (to be

competent), cognitive (to understand/explore), aesthetic (symmetry, order, beauty) and self-actualization.

Q.  Describe principles of personality development.
Personality consists of the distinctive patterns of behavior (including thoughts and emotions) that characterize each
individual’s adaptation to the situations of his or her life.

CHAPTER 20: Psychiatry 1379

There are seven principles of personality development:
1. Cumulative Continuity Principle: Personality traits increase in rank-order consistency as people get older.
2. Maturity Principle: People become better equipped to deal with the demands of life as they acquire experience and skills.
3. Plasticity Principle: Personality can change at any time (but such change may not be easy).
4. Role Continuity Principle: Taking on roles or images can lead personality to be consistent over time.
5. Identity Development Principle: People seek to develop a stable sense of who they are, and then strive to act consistently

with this self-view.
6. Social Investment Principle: Changing social roles at different stages of life, such as becoming a spouse, parent, or boss,

can cause personality change.
7. Corresponsive Principle: Person-environment transactions can cause personality traits to remain consistent or even

magnify over time.
Theories of personality development:
z Sigmund Freud’s dynamics of personality: Human personality is expressed in dealing with conflict between:

Communication is a process by which information and understanding is exchanged between individuals, by any effective
means.

Verbal Communication
z Verbal communication occurs when we engage in speaking with others.
z Can be face-to-face, over the telephone, or online, it is not just about the words, it is also about the caliber and complexity

z Nonverbal communication includes facial expressions, posture, eye contact, hand movements, and touch.

Essential Elements of Communication in Medical Encounters in Accordance with the Kalamazoo Consensus
Statement
The essential elements of physician-patient communication include the following:
a. Open the discussion by:

 Allowing patients to complete their opening statement
 Eliciting the patient’s full set of concerns
 Establishing and maintaining a personal connection

b. Gather information:
 Using open-ended and closed-ended questions appropriately
 By actively listening using nonverbal (eye contact) and verbal (words of encouragement) techniques

 In order to structure, clarify and summarize information.
c. Understand the patient’s perspective by:

 Exploring contextual factors: Age, gender, family, culture, socioeconomic status, spirituality
 Exploring beliefs, concerns, and expectations about health and illness
 Acknowledging and responding to the patient’s ideas, feelings and values

d. Share information:
 Using language, the patient can understand
 By checking for patient’s understanding
 By encouraging questions

e. Reach agreement on problems and plans by:
 Encouraging the patient to participate in decisions to the extent they desire
 Checking the patient’s willingness and ability to follow a plan
 Identifying and enlisting resources and supports

f. Provide closure by:
 Asking if the patient has other issues or concerns
 Summarizing and affirming agreement with the plan of action
 Discussing follow-up (next visit, plan for unexpected outcomes)

Q.  Discuss common mistakes in communicating diagnosis, prognosis and therapy.
Popa-Velea and Purcărea described two major communication flaws most patients complain about: lack of physician
communication skills, and the persistence of an asymmetric therapeutic communicational model. Communication obstacles
brought by the disease itself or by several variables pertaining to the patient, including specific demographic and psychological
contexts, and the sociocultural context are other barriers in communication.
z Lack of physician communication skills or their deterioration throughout the disease: One may have poor

communication skills inherently or due to their upbringing and lack of social interactions during the childhood. This
may have major impact later in life, both social and professional, affecting the doctor-patient relationship significantly in
case of a doctor. Training in medical schools focusing on communication skills and regular practice of talking to patients
following the above essential elements of communication will help overcome this issue.

z The persistence of an asymmetric therapeutic communicational model: It prevents the initial patient from understanding
important facts regarding the causes of disease or function of the medication. This results in poor transmission of information
to the patient, communication during daily therapeutic encounters, and ultimately, a patient’s opinion of the doctor. Such
impressions can have a major impact on the patient’s overall psychological state and frequently the prognosis.

z The particularities of the disease itself: For instance, in many psychological or psychiatric diseases, doctors must deal with
cognitive obstacles (such as the distortion of messages that are exchanged in the therapeutic relationship); in some somatic
conditions, symptoms can impair the patient’s capacity for explanation, listening, or understanding (e.g., pain, neurologic
disorders, etc.).

z The characteristics of the patient: Personality type, for instance, oftentimes offers a highly strict or constrained framework
for the doctor-patient relationship. Patients with personality disorders frequently are unaware of their shortcomings and
put little effort into communicating since they do not anticipate or desire any changes in their way of life. They frequently
use projection as a coping method when they don’t feel understood or supported, therefore they tend to respond by
refusing to follow rules, displaying latent or overt animosity, or transferring unpleasant feelings.

z Demographic variables: Such as age (e.g., elderly people are exposed to limited or distorted communication, via cognitive
impairments or age-illness stereotype). Sociocultural context, which creates a high variability on the way patients express
their suffering and on their focus.

Case: A Letter from the Grave
Respected doctor,
I am writing this letter with extreme sadness. As you may know that it has been three months since my wife and your
patient Mrs. Alka Chaturvedi has passed away. I am writing this letter not with anger or with spite; I am writing this only
with the intent that my wife’s death not be in vain and that the lessons that can be learned from the way you took care of
her may be valuable to other patients in your care and that they will receive the compassion and care from you that Alka
never received.

As you may recall, Alka was diagnosed with breast cancer 5 years ago. We rushed to you knowing your reputation as a
talented oncologist and we were not disappointed. Your aggressive approach to the disease made all the difference. Surgery
and aggressive chemotherapy, while distressing, helped Alka beat the disease and she lived disease-free for 2 years. We were
very happy and were and still are very grateful to you. But fate had ordained that our joy will be short-lived. The disease came
back with a vengeance. Even at this time you did not give up hope and took on the disease like a warrior but then there came
a time that it was clear that the disease had won. We were devastated.

Alka looked up to you as a doctor to provide her with support but it looked like that you were unable to confront the failure.
While you did prescribe pain medications and your office helped us find a home nurse you were reluctant to meet Alka or talk
to her. When we called for appointments, your office would tell us to contact our family doctor for pain medications. When
we did get to see you would not even look at Alka’s eyes. You would distractedly talk to her, refill her pain medications and
dismiss us quickly. It was as if we were seeing a different doctor than the one we had seen when all was well. And when Alka
was admitted to the hospital where she breathed her last you would not even come and see her. We made so many requests
for you to come and visit with her. I even called and told you that it would mean so much for her to see you before she departs
but you did not.

Would it have been too much for you to come and hold her hand for a minute or say a kind word? Doctor—I am not as
learned as you are but patients come to you and repose their faith in you to help them through their illness. We come to you
not with the expectation that a cure is always possible but always with the expectation that you will support us in coping with
the disease and the tremendous effects it has on our lives. We don’t always expect you to succeed but we always expect you
to show us care and compassion. I hate to point to out, doctor, that you abandoned Alka when it was clear that she will not be
a trophy that you can parade as a success. You abandoned Alka and us at the time we needed you most. You sir, abandoned
us when we were most vulnerable.

I write this to you not to fault your knowledge and skills which are considerable. I bear you no ill will. I am grateful that
you gave Alka and our family a few more years of togetherness

Conflicts of interest arise when a practitioner prioritizes their personal interests or benefit over that of the patient. They
introduce prejudice, obstruct wise healthcare decisions, jeopardize clinical results, and also has the potential to erode
confidence and trust.

The physician should continue to offer prompt, appropriate care. The doctor has a moral and legal obligation to attend
to the patient’s requirements as they arise and shouldn’t hand off important tasks to junior staff members. In this situation,
they must make sure the attending clinician is qualified. The doctor should never abandon the patient, and should continue
care until an appropriate transfer is completed. When necessary, they should emphasize the referral’s urgency and make
such referrals easier. They should give all significant and pertinent information when referring. The doctor should only
utilize the patient’s information for that patient’s benefit. By protecting the confidentiality of all information, even that
obtained outside the doctor-patient relationship, the doctor is required to keep this privileged information provided by the
patient in confidence. Although violating confidentiality may not result in immediate bodily injury, it seriously undermines
confidence and trust and harms the partnership. Physicians must refrain from having inappropriate connections with
patients since they are aware of their natural fragility and dependence. Never may a clinician use a patient for financial
gain, or other private interests. Inappropriate relationships cannot be defended by informed consent.

Patients require doctors that are knowledgeable, kind, and trustworthy who prioritize their patients’ needs for a
successful recovery. The therapeutic doctor-patient relationship is a partnership characterized by trust, respect, empathy,
and sincerity.

What is the Failure of Treatment and its Implications for the Doctor-Patient Relationship?
Treatment failure is a complex occurring in all parts of healthcare system. Faulty interaction and communication between
doctor and patients, and between specialities are the most important factors. Other reasons would be patient noncompliance,
nonresponders or disease/organism resistance, doctor’s lack of experience, to name a few.

Insufficient information about the disease and about the treatment including the drug dosage, frequency, adverse effects
and availability of treatment alternatives is to be discussed in detail with the patient during the initial visit. This will help
patient understand what to expect out of the treatment, and enable patient to identify if there is treatment failure allowing
patient to return for change in treatment regimen. This becomes true when the patient takes complete responsibility of
their treatment. The other reasons why one could observe treatment failure is noncompliance to the treatment. The patient
is solely responsible for this. At this point, it is important to involve a family member or a friend in management of the
patient’s disease, by explaining to them about the regimen and importance of it. Certain patients may not respond to a type
of treatment (e.g., due to inherent inability to convert drug into active form). Some diseases may be resistant to certain drugs,
like in steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome for example, or in certain infections caused by the organisms that are resistant
to the chemotherapeutic agent(s). Following guidelines and understanding the protocols will help in determining the next
line of treatment in these patients. The health service center will take complete responsible for patients who have had severe
complaints despite following all recommendations, or when the patient is admitted to the center for an illness or to undergo
a procedure. It falls into the hands of the center, through the healthcare workers, to help patients achieve treatment goals. The
doctor involved in the treatment of the patient should be competent

What is Empathy and Patient Care?
Empathy is frequently described as “feeling as others,” yet its worth has been disputed. The notion of empathy in the medical
field has been contested by academics; some contend that clinical empathy is restricted to a purely cognitive comprehension
of emotional states, while others contend that clinical empathy should represent the humane intent of medicine. It appears
that objectivity, emotional distance, and detached concern are all inclusive and leave no or insufficient room for the human
aspects of illness. It has been demonstrated that this phenomenon has detrimental effects on both patients and healthcare
professionals.

Objectivity, detached concern and emotional distance care are hallmarks of mainstream medical culture. The medical
profession has become overly focused on science at the expense of the human aspects of disease and multifaceted components.
Clinical empathy has been defined as the ability to observe emotions in others, the ability to feel those emotions, and finally
the ability to respond to those emotions. The empathic communicative response goes beyond verbal expression. Nonverbal
communication includes body language, such as tone of voice, facial emotions, posture, and natural gestures. Clinical
empathy includes a thorough cognitive and sensory comprehension of the patient’s feelings. As a result, it is neither total
immersion in the experience of the other nor emotional detachment.

Patients have expressed a desire for caregivers to be more approachable. It makes an effort to move medicine in the
direction of a relationship-centered care model, where the human element is crucial and patients’ experiences are valued. In
this case, therapeutic empathy is seen as a way to support patients’ emotional experience and expression. Clinical empathy
benefits people on many different levels by fostering communication, trust, and understanding. Generally speaking, it has
been shown that providing empathic care increases autonomy, lowers emotional discomfort, and improves therapeutic
outcomes and patient satisfaction of care. Positive clinical outcomes, including patient adherence to the treatment plan
and interest in medical advice, are produced through empathic patient care. Empathy has also been found to aid patients’
comprehension of available treatments and involvement in therapeutic decision-making.

Terminating a therapeutic relationship can be particularly challenging and onerous for the treating medical practitioner.
A practitioner may want to end the connection for a variety of reasons, from inappropriate behavior and violence to legal
action. When ending this, due regard for their professional and legal obligation should be made. Generally, the relationship
ceases by mutual agreement for reasons like the patient moving to a new place or no longer needing therapy. The patient
might be referred to another doctor who will take over their care. Even though these situations not problematic, they should
nonetheless be thoroughly documented.

The patient must be fully informed of the clinician’s decision, and preparations must be made to maintain continuity
of care, including the dissemination of pertinent clinical information. This point of view seems to have assisted in the
identification of a number of practical requirements that must be met in order to successfully end the therapeutic partnership
without violating ethical and legal commitments. There must be records of all communications and meetings in the patient’s
file. Poor health outcome or a patient filing a lawsuit alleging an unreasonable refusal to treat could result from inadequate
communication paired with a failure to establish clear boundaries to conclude the relationship amicably.

What is Hospice Care?
Hospice care consists of palliative care provided at the end of life that provides comprehensive comfort care for patients
and support for family members. This includes offering the patient the medical care, pain management, and emotional and
spiritual support they desire and need. According to the eligibility requirements, a doctor must conclude that the patient’s
prognosis calls for an anticipated life expectancy of 6 months or less if the illness progresses as expected. When hospice care
best satisfies a patient’s objectives, family physicians can be important allies in assisting patients and family members with
the transition. An interdisciplinary team that includes family doctors, physician medical directors, nurses, social workers,
counselors, home health aides, and skilled volunteers provides hospice care.

Although where hospice care is typically administered in patient’s house, when symptom control is required, hospice
care may also be given in long-term care institutions, hospice facilities, and hospitals. In comparison to normal treatment,
hospice care has been linked to improved symptom relief, better fulfilment of patients’ end-of-life desires, and higher overall
ratings of the quality of end-of-life care. Family doctors are best suited to handle and organize patients’ needs for hospice care.

Can Patients Choose to Die? Is there a Role for Doctors in the Death of Patients? Can Doctors Assist Death?
Before the Mental Healthcare Act, which became effective in 2018, attempted suicide was a crime punishable under Section
309 of the Indian Penal Code. The statute calls on governments to offer mental healthcare and rehabilitation rather than
punishment. The idea of the “right to die” is founded on the notion that everyone has the right to end their life or submit to
voluntary euthanasia. When a person has this right, it is frequently assumed that they use assisted suicide, or decline life-
prolonging treatment if they have a terminal illness or lack the will to live. But this concept of “right to die” is debated for time
now.

The doctor assumes the role in assisting a patient during euthanasia. Euthanasia is practice of intentionally ending life to
eliminate pain and suffering. It can be passive or active. Passive euthanasia is when patient’s life support measures necessary
to continue one’s life expectancy are withdrawn. Active euthanasia entails use of active lethal substance to end one’s life.
In India, passive euthanasia was legalized in 2018. The decision was made as part of the judgment in a case concerning
Aruna Shanbaug, who passed away in 2015 after being in a persistent vegetative state. The Supreme Court specified two

in a persistent vegetative state for whom the feed can be tapered out and pain-managing palliatives be added, according to

How Should Doctors Deal with the Emotions of Patients and Family Facing Death?
The five stages of dying by Kubler-Ross are as follows:
1. Denial is a protective mechanism used by patients who initially deny the truth of a fatal prognosis. It’s critical to

communicate facts clearly and give them time to comprehend the news.
2. Anger: Patients may vent their wrath at their doctors, their families, or even spiritual beings. Recognizing anger as a

normal emotion enables loved ones and medical professionals to react with sensitivity.
3. Bargaining: Which may be reasonable or based on magical thinking, is a means through which patients attempt to acquire

some control over their sickness. Caretakers should exercise caution to avoid misleading patients or engaging in excessive
patient bargaining.

4. Depression: Patients with depression report feeling down, worn out, and uninterested. Caretakers must practice
compassion again while acknowledging that these behaviors are a normal part of the grieving process.

5. Acceptance: Patients accept the reality of their condition and concentrate on having fun in the time they have left. Making
peace with their situation and future planning take precedence. Empathy and support should be given at every level of
the process because acceptance may not always be healthier than other phases.

What Does the Patient Experience When He/She is Dying? Can Physicians Make the Process of Death
Comfortable?
Dying experiences vary for individuals. Some find it peaceful, with periods of recognition and consciousness followed by
lapses. Changes in color, circulation, and breathing start occurring. Gradually, the person will enter complete unconsciousness
while still potentially able to hear and sense their surroundings. Restlessness may accompany the dying process for some
individuals, but such symptoms can typically be managed with palliative care. During these stages, the palliative care
team will provide increased support. Being present for a dying person can make a significant difference. Sitting with them,
holding their hand, or speaking calmly and reassuringly can bring great comfort. These seemingly simple acts should not be
underestimated, even if the person does not respond.

For everyone involved, the change from treatment to end-of-life care presents difficulties. Healthcare professionals
could believe that their job is done and stop attending to the patient, causing them and their loved ones to feel abandoned.
When death is near, patients and their families frequently seek advice on the psychological and physiological changes that
take place. It is possible for caregivers to provide support and direction during this process by being aware of the stages of
mourning. Patients and family need clear explanations from medical professionals to understand terminal disease and deal
with considerable loss. To encourage healing and resilience, healthcare professionals also need to be able to manage their
own grief.

What are the Emotions Faced by Doctors When Confronting Death in Patients? Is Death a Defeat for the
Doctor? Should the Doctor be Emotionally Detached from a Dying Patient? 
The loss of a patient they were familiar with or the circumstances surrounding the death may have an impact on doctors. They
might be experiencing related sentiments of insecurity, helplessness, shame, or failure, or they might be fearful of criticism
as a result of their engagement in the patient’s treatment. Inattentiveness, impatience, irritability, mental exhaustion, and
burnout are the results of the unrecognized grief. Doctors’ ability to deliver high-quality care will suffer as a result of the
professional taboo surrounding grief.

1390 CHAPTER 21: AETCOM—Attitude, Ethics and Communication Manual

A sudden death produces a feeling of shock-and self-doubt. A doctor who is affected by a patient’s death may find it
difficult to cope when subject to an investigation by their employer or the Medical Council and find this particularly worrying
as it may attract further scrutiny and criticism. The doctor may be required to attend an inquest as a witness or to prepare a
report for a significant event inquiry or the coroner. The family could file a complaint or file a lawsuit. The mere prospect of
these occurrences will make the doctor anxious and stressed.

For doctors who deal with death on a regular basis, they should understand that death is an inevitable aspect of life. But
on occasion, it can have a bad impact on a doctor’s mental health. As a result, doctors should never feel ashamed to ask for
assistance when they need it or to use the available counselling services. Any doctor can be surprised by how a death affects
them sometimes, and they should be aware that it is acceptable to feel this way.

No matter the circumstances, dealing with death is frequently painful, and doctors learn coping mechanisms throughout
their careers. It may be helpful to be able to compartmentalize sadness over a patient’s passing from other elements of life
and work. This will help cope with the event better.

What are the Cultural Aspects of Dying?
Although death is a universal experience, grieving habits are very much influenced by culture. All cultures have established
polite means of coping with death because it is a common occurrence in life, and tampering with these customs can make it
difficult for people to deal while they are grieving. It is crucial for healthcare professionals to understand certain fundamentals
about how various cultures may approach and deal with death, even while it is unrealistic to expect them to be familiar with
each family’s specific grieving rituals and traditions. There are important topics that, despite being challenging, must be
covered in interactions between doctors, nurses, and families.

It seems logical that delivering culturally sensitive grief and end-of-life care causes discomfort for healthcare practitioners.
The difficulties of being professionally suitable and sympathetic are undoubtedly made more difficult by linguistic and cultural
obstacles. Despite the fact that patients and families may want sympathy, counsel, and direction from doctors and nurses,
the realities of a scenario frequently entail a rush for time and both physical and emotional tiredness among caregivers and
families. Sometimes, when important judgments need to be taken, we just don’t show enough warmth and sensitivity in the
moment. For individuals with training in the Western Medical Tradition, the clinical facts call for rapid and rational reasoning.
Such a straight approach could appear harsh to people from many cultures, and decisions about things like organ donation
might be seen as cruel right away after someone passes away. In some cultures, mourners are expected to express their sorrow,
including wailing, because the more anguish is shown and the more people grieve, the more the deceased was loved. Other
cultures expect moderation. If a doctor breaks news about a terminal illness to a patient directly, family members may react
badly in many cultures. Patients and families may respect the right to privacy highly. Carteret suggests asking the following

INTRODUCTION
Immune system is defined as the body’s defense system that protects against pathogenic microorganisms and noninfectious
foreign substances.

Immune system is the third line of defense against infection (Fig. 22.1). Innate and adaptive are the two types of immune
response.

DUALITY OF IMMUNE SYSTEM
Humoral (Antibody-mediated) Immunity
z It involves production of antibodies against foreign antigens, by a subset of lymphocytes called B-cells. These B cells are

stimulated to form plasma cells and they secrete antibodies.
z Humoral immunity is involved in defense against bacteria, bacterial toxins, and viruses that circulate freely in body fluids,

before they enter cells. They are also responsible for certain reactions against transplanted tissue.

Cell-mediated Immunity
Q.  Write short note on cell-mediated immunity.
z It involves specialized set of lymphocytes called T-cells that recognize foreign antigens on the surface of cells, organisms,

or tissues: Helper T-cells and cytotoxic T-cells.
z Defense against:

 Bacteria and viruses which lie inside the host cells and are not accessible to antibodies.
 Fungi, protozoa, and helminths, cancer cells, transplanted tissue.

Antigens
Most of the antigens are proteins or large polysaccharides from a foreign microbes or nonmicrobes:
z Microbes: The antigens may be capsules, cell walls, toxins, viral capsids, flagella, etc.
z Nonmicrobes: These antigens include pollen, egg white, serum proteins, and surface molecules of red blood cell and

transplanted tissue.
Lipids and nucleic acids become antigen only when combined with proteins or polysaccharides.

CYTOKINES
Q.  Write short note on cytokines.
The immune response involves multiple interactions between many cells. These cells are lymphocytes, dendritic cells,
macrophages, other inflammatory cells (e.g., neutrophils), and endothelial cells. Few of these interactions are due to cell-to-
cell contact. However, many interactions and effector functions of leukocytes are mediated by short-acting soluble proteins:
multipurpose chemical messengers called cytokines. Cytokines which mediate communications between leukocytes are
called interleukins.

Mode of Action
Cytokines exert their effect by binding to specific receptors on target cells. They may act by three ways:
1. Autocrine when the cytokines act on the same cells which secrete them.
2. Paracrine when cytokines are produced by one cell type which act on adjacent/nearby target cells.
3. Endocrine when the cytokines secreted into the circulation act on target cells at a site distant from their site of synthesis.

Interleukins
z They are produced by and signal between white cells which mediate endocrine communication at a site distant from their

site of synthesis.
z Source: Activated macrophages.
z Effects: Fever, bone marrow release of neutrophils into circulation (leukocytosis), B-cell proliferation, antibody

production, and production of IL-2 by T-cells. Interleukin-2 (IL-2) stimulates the proliferation of activated B-cells,
T-cells, and NK cells.

Tumor Necrosis Factor-a
z Source: TNF-α is produced by activated macrophages in response to infection by bacteria and other microbes.
z Effects: Fever, cachexia (pathologic state characterized by weight loss and anorexia seen in neoplastic diseases and some

chronic infections), anorexia, shock, enhanced leukocyte cytotoxicity, enhanced NK-cell function, acute phase protein
synthesis, proinflammatory cytokine induction, increases apoptosis, and expression of cytokines and adhesion molecules.

Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate
Q.  Write short note on erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR).
z It is the rate at which red blood cells (RBCs) settle down when anticoagulated whole blood is allowed to stand.
z RBCs have net negative charge on their surface and do not aggregate but tend to repel each other. Plasma proteins have

positive charge and neutralize the surface negative charge called Zeta potential of red cells.

Factors Affecting ESR
Plasma factors: Increase in certain plasma proteins (especially fibrinogen), reduces the repulsive forces between the red
blood cells and cause them to stack together like tyres, or rouleaux. Rouleaux have more mass/surface area ratio than single
red cells, and therefore sediment faster and increase the ESR.
z An accelerated ESR is favored by elevated levels of fibrinogen, globulins, and cholesterol (which increase the positive

charge of plasma) whereas albumin and lecithin retard ESR.
z Elevated fibrinogen and raised ESR are also observed in pregnancy, old age, and end-stage renal disease.
z In acute inflammation ESR and acute phase reactants are raised.
z ESR is increased in conditions associated with monoclonal (multiple myeloma) or polyclonal (chronic infections like

tuberculosis) increase in immunoglobulins. In systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), ESR is raised but CRP may be normal.
Red cell factors: The sedimentation rate is directly proportional to the weight of the cell aggregates and inversely proportional to the
surface area. ESR may be low if plasma proteins are low or red cell morphology is abnormal making rouleaux formation impossible.
z Anemia increases the ESR and polycythemia decreases it.
z Microcytes sedimentation is slower than macrocytes.
z Red cells with an abnormal or irregular shape, such as sickle cells or spherocytes, do not exhibit rouleaux formation and

have low ESR.
Normal range: For men 1–10 mm 1st hour and for women 5–20 mm 1st hour.

COMPLEMENT SYSTEM
Q.  Write short note on the complement system.
z The complement system is a group of plasma proteins (Ω globulins), major source being the liver. C1q produced mainly

by bone marrow derived cells like macrophages and dendritic cells.
z They are proteases and are important in both inflammation and immunity.

Pathways of Complement System Activation (Fig. 22.3)
The decisive step in complement activation is the proteolysis of the third component, C3. Cleavage of C3 can occur by any
one of three pathways:
1. Classical pathway: It is activated by antigen-antibody (Ag-Ab) complexes in which C1 binds to antibody (IgM or IgG),

acute phase proteins, charged molecules, and apoptotic or necrotic cell debris.

FIG. 22.3: Different pathways of activation and functions of the complement system. All pathways of activation lead to cleavage of C3.

1396 CHAPTER 22: Immunology

2. Alternative pathway: This pathway is antibody-independent.
 It is activated by binding of C3 directly to microbial surface molecules [e.g., endotoxin, or lipopolysaccharides (LPS)],

complex polysaccharides, cobra venom, and “altered self” such as tumor cells, in the absence of antibody. They
cleave C3 to C3b.

 C3b in the presence of factors B and D generates C3bBb (alternative pathway C3 convertase).
 C3bBb is labile and degraded by factors I and H, but stabilized by properdin and can subsequently activate C3.
 This results in persistent and prolonged C3 activation and hypocomplementemia. In addition, decreased synthesis of

C3 by the liver is also responsible for hypocomplementemia.
3. Lectin pathway: It directly activates C1 when plasma mannose-binding lectin (MBL) binds to mannose on microbes.

Q.  List the clinical features of IgG4-related diseases.
Immunoglobulin G4-related Disease (IgG4-RD)
IgG4-RD is an immune-mediated fibroinflammatory condition affecting multiple organs.

The hallmarks of IgG4-RD are dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrations with predominance of IgG4-positive plasma
cells in the affected tissue, as accompanied by some degree of fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis and increased number of
eosinophils.

Clinical Manifestations
Four main clinical phenotypes have been identified.
1. Group 1: Pancreato-hepato-biliary disease
2. Group 2: Retroperitoneal fibrosis/aortitis
3. Group 3: Head and neck limited disease
4. Group 4: Classic Mikulicz syndrome with systemic involvement.

Common manifestations of IgG4-RD include the following, type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis and IgG4-related sclerosing
cholangitis, Mikulicz disease, Riedel’s thyroiditis, interstitial pneumonitis, and tubulointerstitial nephritis.

Tissue biopsy is the gold standard for the diagnosis
which reveals tumor-like swelling of involved organs, a Treatment
lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate enriched in IgG4-positive plasma • Glucocorticoids-prednisone
cells, variable degree of fibrosis that has a characteristic • Rituximab, azathioprine, and methotrexate.

Allergy
Q.  Define allergy. List atopic disorders.
z Allergy is defined as a hypersensitivity reaction induced by exposure to an otherwise harmless exogenous substance

(known as an allergen), generally environmental.
z In an allergic reaction, initial exposure to allergen triggers the production of specific IgE antibodies by activated B-cells.

These IgE antibodies bind to the surface of mast cells via high-affinity IgE receptors.
z The first dose of allergen (priming dose) sensitizes the immunologic system (B lymphocyte). On re-exposure, the allergen

(shocking dose) binds to membrane-bound IgE which activates the mast cells, releasing vasoactive mediators (the early
phase response), and causing a type I hypersensitivity reaction and the symptoms of allergy. This may be followed by late
phase reaction and is mediated by basophils, eosinophils, and macrophages.

z Examples: Asthma, anaphylaxis, rhinitis, urticaria, angioedema, eczema, and food hypersensitivity.

Angioedema
Q.  Write short essay/note on the clinical features and treatment of angioedema.
Angioedema is defined as a well-demarcated localized edema involving the deeper layers of the skin, including the
subcutaneous tissue and submucosal tissues.

Etiology
It is an IgE-mediated reaction that causes direct release of histamine from the mast cells. It follows a variety of allergens. It may
develop due to insect sting, drug reaction, food allergy, and exposure to other biological products. Rarely, angiotensin-converting
enzyme (ACE) inhibitors may produce angioedema due to increased levels of bradykinin. Most of the cases are idiopathic.

C1-esterase Inhibitor Deficiency
C1-esterase (C1INH) inhibitor is a complement protein that inhibits spontaneous activation of classical complement pathway.
C1-esterase inhibitor also regulates kinin cascade, activation of which increases local bradykinin levels and produces local
pain and swelling. Both C1-esterase inhibitor and C1 levels are low. C1INH deficiency produces bradykinin. Deficiency of
C1INH may be hereditary or acquired disorder.
z Hereditary angioedema: It is an autosomal dominant disorder, is due to C1 esterase inhibitor (C1INH) deficiency.

Angioedema develops either spontaneously or following infection or injury (e.g., dental injury). Onset is usually in
early childhood. The attacks become worse at puberty and usually its frequency and severity decreases after the age of

Q.  Write short note on treatment of anaphylaxis. List life-saving drugs used in anaphylactic shock.

Treatment
Anaphylaxis is an acute medical emergency and its early recognition is imperative, since death occurs within minutes to hours after the first
symptoms.
• Prevent further contact with allergen, e.g., removal of bee sting.
• Ensure airway patency: Fatal outcomes in anaphylaxis are mainly due to either airway constriction or hypotension.
• Oxygen alone via a nasal catheter or with nebulized salbutamol/albuterol, oxygen 4–6 L/min.

– If progressive hypoxia develops, either endotracheal intubation or tracheostomy with intermittent positive ventilation is required for
oxygen delivery.

• Administer adrenaline (epinephrine) intramuscularly into the thigh and is the most critical drug to administer. Earlier administration
during the course of an anaphylactic event is better.
– Adult: 0.3–0.5 mg (0.3–0.5 mL of a 1:1,000 solution) IM in the lateral thigh, repeated at 10- to 15-minute intervals if necessary.
– Child: 1:1,000 dilution at 0.01 mg/kg or 0.1–0.3 mL administered IM in the lateral thigh, repeated at 10- to 15-minute intervals if

necessary.
◆ 0.5 mL of 1:1,000 solution sublingually in cases of major airway compromise or hypotension.
◆ 3–5 mL of 1:10,000 solution via central line.
◆ 3–5 mL of 1:10,000 solution diluted with 10 mL of normal saline via endotracheal tube.
◆ For protracted symptoms that require multiple doses of epinephrine, an IV epinephrine drip may be useful; the infusion is titrated

to maintain adequate BP.
• Administer antihistamines: They may prevent the progression of urticaria and pruritus, but does not reverse hypotension or tissue

edema by directly opposing effects of mast cell activation, e.g., chlorphenamine 10 mg IM or slow IV injection, diphenhydramine, 50–100
mg IM or IV.

• Administer corticosteroids: Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV stat (not effective for the acute event as it takes 4 hours to act; but alleviate
recurrence of bronchospasm, urticaria, and hypotension).

• Glucagon could reverse refractory bronchospasm and hypotension in patients who are taking b-adrenergic antagonists. Recommended
dosage is 1–5 mg intravenously bolus slowly over 5 minutes followed by an infusion at 5–15 µg/min titrated to

Q.  Write short note on serum sickness.
z It is a systemic immune complex-mediated disease (type III hypersensitivity reaction).
z It was a frequent sequelae to the administration of large amounts of foreign serum (e.g., serum from immunized horses

used for protection against diphtheria). But nowadays it is infrequent.
z IgG is produced when a foreign antigen is injected in large quantities. They form soluble immune (antigen-antibody)

complexes.

Introduction of antigen → body’s immune system responds by synthesizing antibodies after 4–10 days → antibody reacts
with antigen, forming soluble complexes that may diffuse into vascular walls and may initiate activation of complement →
complement-containing immune complexes generate influx of leukocytes into vessel walls—proteolytic enzymes that can
mediate tissue damage are released → immune complex deposition + inflammatory responses are responsible for vasculitic
lesions seen. Box 22.9: Lesion produced in acute serum sickness.

z Cardiac amyloidosis: The heart is the second most
commonly (50%) affected organ and may show concentric

Other Amyloids
z Cerebral amyloidosis: Brain is a common site of amyloid deposition, though it is not directly affected in any form of

acquired systemic amyloidosis.
z Alzheimer’s disease: Intracerebral and cerebrovascular amyloid deposits are found in Alzheimer’s disease. Most cases

are sporadic.
z Transmissible spongiform encephalopathy: In hereditary spongiform encephalopathies, several amyloid plaques are

Q.  Write short essay/note on various types (classification) of chromosomal disorders/aberrations.
Classification of Chromosomal Disorders (Box 23.1)
Numerical Chromosomal Aberrations
Normal cells are diploid containing 46 chromosomes, 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes. The 23 chromosomes
(22 autosomes and one sex chromosome) constitute a haploid. Any exact multiple of the haploid number is called euploid.
Types of numerical aberrations
Aneuploidy: It is defined as a chromosome number that is not a multiple of 23 (the normal haploid number). It is caused by
either loss or gain of one or more chromosomes. Aneuploidy may result from nondisjunction or anaphase lag.
z Trisomy: Numerical abnormalities with the presence of one extra chromosome are referred to as trisomy (2n + 1). It may

involve either sex chromosomes or autosomes. Examples: Down syndrome (patients have three copies of chromosome
21, i.e., 47 XX, +21, hence Down syndrome is often known as trisomy 21), Patau syndrome (trisomy 13; 47 XY, +13), and
Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18; 47 XY, +18).

z Monosomy: Numerical abnormalities with the absence or loss of one chromosome (2n – 1) are referred to as monosomy.
It may involve autosomes or sex chromosomes. Monosomy of autosomes is almost incompatible with survival. Example:
For monosomy of sex chromosomes is Turner syndrome (45 XO) instead of normal XX (46 XX).

Polyploidy: It is chromosome number that is a multiple greater Box 23.1: Types of chromosomal abnormality.
than two of the haploid number (multiples of haploid number 23). Numerical abnormalities
Triploidy is three times the haploid number (69), tetraploidy is four • Aneuploidy
times the haploid number (92). Polyploidy is incompatible with life – Monosomy
and usually results in spontaneous abortion. – Trisomy

Types of Structural/Chromosomal Aberrations (Figs. 23.1A to H)
Translocations: It is a structural alteration between two chromosomes in which a segment of one chromosome gets
detached and is transferred to another chromosome. There are two types of translocations:
1. Balanced reciprocal translocations: It is characterized by single break in each of the two chromosomes with exchange

of genetic material distal to the break. There is no loss of genetic material. A balanced reciprocal translocation between
the long arm of chromosome 5 and the short arm of chromosome 10 would be written 46, XX, t (5; 10) (q31; p14).
 Simple translocation: In this case, terminal segment of a chromosome is integrated at one end of a nonhomologous

region. Simple translocations are rather rare.
 Shift: In shift, an intercalary segment of a chromosome is integrated within a nonhomologous chromosome.

2. Robertsonian translocation/centric fusion:
 This results from the breakage of two acrocentric chromosomes (i.e., chromosome 13, 14, 15, 21, 22) at or close to

their centromeres and subsequent fusion of their long arms.
 The short arms of each chromosome are lost, this being of no clinical importance as they contain genes only for

ribosomal RNA, for which there are multiple copies on various other chromosomes.
 The total chromosome number is reduced to 45.
 The overall incidence of this translocation is 1 in 1,000, the most common being 13q14q.
 The major practical importance is that this can predispose to the birth of babies with Down syndrome.

Inversion: When a segment of chromosome is oriented in the reverse direction, such segment said to be inverted and the
phenomenon is termed as inversion.
Isochromosomes: They are formed due to faulty centromere division. Normally, centromeres divide in a plane parallel to
long axis of the chromosome. If a centromere divides in a plane transverse to the long axis, it results in pair of isochromosomes.
One pair consists of two short arms and the other of two long arms.
Deletion: It is the loss of a part of a chromosome. It is of two types namely: (1) interstitial (middle) and (2) terminal (rare).
z Interstitial deletion: It occurs when there are two breaks within a chromosome arm. This is followed by loss of the

chromosomal material between the breaks and fusion of the broken ends of the remaining portion of the chromosome.
It has to be specified in which region(s) and at what bands the breaks have occurred. For example, 46, XY, del (16)

DOWN SYNDROME (TRISOMY 21)
Q.  PE32.1 Discuss the genetic basis, risk factors, complications, prenatal diagnosis, management and genetic counseling
in Down’s syndrome.
The best known and most common chromosome related syndrome. Formerly known as “Mongolism”.

It is the most common chromosomal disorder and is a leading cause of mental retardation. The incidence of Down syndrome
in newborns is about 1 in 700 live births.

Etiology and Pathogenesis
z Maternal age: It has a strong influence on the incidence of trisomy 21. Children of older mothers have much greater risk

of having Down syndrome. The risk for mothers < 25 years of age to have the trisomy is about 1 in 1,500 births. At 40 years
of age, 1 in 100 births. At 45 years, 1 in 40 births.

z Other factors: Increased incidence may be associated with exposure of mother to pesticides, electromagnetic fields,
anesthetic drugs, alcohol, and caffeine.

Mechanism of trisomy 21: The three copies of chromosome 21 in somatic cells cause Down syndrome. It may be due to:
1. About 95% of these individuals have nondisjunction during the first meiotic division of gametogenesis.
2. Robertsonian translocation of an extra long arm of chromosome 21 to another acrocentric chromosome causes about 5%

of cases.
3. About 1% mosaicism having two different cell lines, one with normal chromosomal constitution and the other with an

extra chromosome 21.

z Flat face and occiput, with a low-bridged nose, reduced interpupillary distance and oblique palpebral fissures.
z Epicanthal folds of the eyes impart an almond shape to the eyes and an oriental appearance (obsolete term mongolism).
z A speckled appearance of the iris (brushfield spots), enlarged and malformed ears.
z A protruding furrowed tongue (macroglossia), which typically lacks a central fissure and protrudes through an open

mouth (scrotal tongue).

with hypoplastic mid phalanx (60%), short stature, hypotonia and space between the first and second toes (sandal gap).

dislocation.

genetic band in 21q22 critical region is considered responsible for the cardiac anomalies. Complete atrioventricular septal

Q.  Discuss autosomal recessive inheritance with examples.

Autosomal Recessive Pattern of Inheritance
z Autosomal recessive inheritance involves mutations in both copies of a gene.
z These disorders generally manifest when both the homologous chromosomes carry mutant genes (homozygous state).
The general features of these disorders are:
z Location of mutant gene: These genes are located on autosomes.
z Required number of defective gene: Symptoms of the disease appear only when an individual has two copies of the

mutant gene. The heterozygote state is called as a carrier. In the carrier state, the product of the normal gene is able to
compensate for the mutant allele and is hence the patients are asymptomatic.

z Horizontal transmission: The observation of multiple affected members of kindred in the same generation, but no
affected family members in other generations.

z Pattern of inheritance: For a child to be at risk, both parents must be having at least one copy of the mutant gene. Almost
all inborn errors of metabolism are autosomal recessive disorders.

z Sex affected: Males and females being equally affected, though some traits exhibit different expression in males and
females (ovarian cancer, hypospadias).

z Consanguineous marriage: It is common predisposing factor.
z Recurrence risk of 25% for parents with a previous affected child.
z Risks of transmission (Figs. 23.6A to E) to children (offspring):

 When both parents are heterozygous for the condition: Heterozygous parents carry one mutated gene and normal
gene. When two heterozygotes mate, 25% of the children will be affected, 50% will be unaffected heterozygotes and
25% will be normal.

Q.  Discuss X-linked inheritance with examples.
Almost all sex-linked Mendelian disorders are X-linked. Males with mutations affecting the Y-linked genes are usually infertile.
Expression of an X-linked disorder is different in males and females. Though X-linked disorders may be inherited either as
dominant or recessive, almost all X-linked disorders have recessive pattern of inheritance.
Characteristics of X-linked inheritance:
z Males are more commonly and more severely affected than females.
z Female carriers are generally unaffected, or if affected, they are affected more mildly than males.
z Affected males will have only carrier daughters.
z Carrier women have a 25% risk for having an affected son, a 25% risk for a carrier daughter, and a 50% chance for a child

that does not inherit the mutated X-linked gene.

X-linked Recessive Traits
z Location of mutant gene: Mutant gene is on the X chromosome and there is no male-to-male transmission.
z Required number of defective gene: One copy of mutant gene is required for the manifestation of disease in males, but

two copies of the mutant gene are needed in females.
z Sex affected: Males are more frequently affected and manifest disease than females; daughters of affected male are all

asymptomatic carriers. In many diseases, males do not survive.
z Pattern of inheritance (Figs. 23.7A to D): Transmission is through female carrier (heterozygous). Mothers are always

carriers and all their sons are affected. The disease is never passed from father to son.
z Very rarely, a female can develop the disease due to:

 Female having Turner syndrome (XO) with only one X chromosome.
 Presence of testicular feminization syndrome.

GENE THERAPY
Q.  Write short note on gene therapy.

Definition: Gene therapy is the insertion of genes into an individual’s cells and tissues to treat a disease, such as a hereditary
disease in which a deleterious mutant allele is replaced with a functional one.

To be effective, the gene therapy requires methods that ensure the safe, efficient and stable introduction of genes into
human cells. Gene therapy uses genes to treat or prevent disease. First done on September 14, 1990 for Ashanthi DeSilva
suffering from severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) where the missing gene introduced through processed WBC.

Approaches for Correcting Faulty Genes
z A normal gene may be inserted into a nonspecific location to replace a nonfunctional gene.
z An abnormal gene could be swapped through homologous recombination.
z Repair through selective reverse mutation.
z The regulation of a particular gene could be altered.

CHAPTER 23: Genetics 1429

Types of Gene Therapy
The cells in the body can be divided into two main categories: (1) somatic cells and (2) germ cells.
1. Somatic cell therapy: It involves delivering a correcting gene to somatic cells in the affected tissues. Somatic cells are the

nonreproductive cells and its therapeutic effect ends with the individual receiving it and is not passed on to the future
generations. Hence, somatic cell therapy is considered as a safer approach. This type of gene therapy is used for disorders
such as cystic fibrosis, muscular dystrophy, cancers, and certain infectious diseases.

2. Germ cell therapy: In germ cell therapy, germ cells (egg or sperms) are used and it results in permanent changes that
are passed on to the future generations. Thus, it offers the possibility of permanently eliminating some diseases from a
particular family and ultimately from the population. It is not accepted at present due to ethical reasons.

Arguments for Germline Gene Therapy
z Medical utility: The potential of a true “cure”.
z Medical necessity: May be only way to cure some diseases.
